body.text: Secretary-General António Guterres joins a virtual meeting on climate challenges (Loey Felipe/UN Photo)
Australia and the next UN chief need each other
As António Guterres’ term ends amid crisis, Australia has the history – and the interest – to support his successor.

When Prime Minister Albanese joins global leaders next week at the High-Level segment of the UN General Assembly, one issue will dominate the gathering: the selection of the next Secretary-General. António Guterres’ term ends on 31 December and the race for his succession is underway. For now, there is no front-runner, and lack of agreement by year’s end, is a possibility. Australia should follow closely.

Meanwhile, global armed conflict reached a record high. This is a result of the disintegrating world order, which is also driving the UN’s demise. As conflict proliferates and the UN proves unable to respond, its legitimacy erodes further, and the international system grows more unstable and violent still – a multilateral doom loop.

This has direct implications for Australia, with its defence spending projected to rise to 3% of GDP by 2033, an additional $117 billion over a decade. The calls for enhancing defence spending in a lawless world are understandable, and could help restore a balance of power. But when everybody rearms, this also increases the risk of conflict.
There is a need to reinvest in the world’s “shock absorbers” too: institutions like the UN that have helped defuse major conflict.

Addressing today’s global crisis, and echoing Fullilove’s 2025 speech, Prime Minister Mark Carney said that the world is living through “a rupture, not a transition” in the international order that provided a modicum of stability for middle powers such as Canada and Australia. His answer was to stop “living within a lie” about a rules-based order and build what he terms “variable geometry”: coalitions of the willing to tackle different problems.
Since the UN Charter gives the Secretary-General little formal power, the office depends almost entirely on the political acumen and the strength of the incumbent’s personality.

Carney's approach is reasonable. But he did not explain how these coalitions should work. In fact, there is no need to reinvent the wheel. Australia has already built such coalitions within the UN: for example, in Bougainville between 1998 and 2003, when it led a small regional coalition, working in tandem with a UN political office to end the civil war. Working through the UN provides many benefits, including legitimacy and reach. It is also inexpensive in comparison to defence spending. Recent attempts to bypass the UN, such as the Trump administration’s Board of Peace, have shown the limits of those approaches.
But can the UN fulfill such a role again?

When an institution is in crisis, it matters even more who leads it. Since the UN Charter gives the Secretary-General little formal power, the office depends almost entirely on the political acumen and the strength of the incumbent’s personality. A Secretary-General who builds trust with all member states, keeps communication open in a crisis, and speaks with charisma and authority can get things done. History shows this matters even more when the Security Council is deadlocked, as Hammarskjöld’s mission to Beijing demonstrated.

To renew the organisation, the next Secretary-General will have to build coalitions in its support, to engage personally in restoring its diplomatic role, and to illustrate to the public its worth. That person will probably hail from Latin America and will have catching-up to do on Asia, where most of humanity, the global economy, and security players are. Unlike Guterres, who did not visit Australia, the new Secretary-General will have to travel early and widely, to build standing and relationships. The next Secretary-General will need Australia’s backing.

Australia can build on this record right now. Albanese’s presence in New York next week is a chance to lobby the Security Council to ensure the race for the job culminates successfully. Afterwards, Australia can draw on coalitions like MIKTA – a grouping of five middle powers comprising Mexico, Indonesia, South Korea, Türkiye, and Australia – to bolster the new Secretary-General’s efforts to revitalise the organisation. A Council seat for the 2029–30 term, which Australia is campaigning for, would be an opportunity to do even more.

In 1949, Australia’s H.V. Evatt, serving as President of the UN General Assembly, called the UN “the corner-stone of effective international action to maintain peace and security and promote higher standards of welfare throughout the whole world.” Australia helped build the UN’s foundations. It has every reason to defend it now.

Daniel Safran-Hon is a non-resident senior adviser at the International Peace Institute (IPI) in New York. He previously served with the UN in the Executive Office of the Secretary-General and in UN missions in Africa and the Middle East.
